requirements.requirement: At least 512 MB of compressed in-memory (zram) swap configured on node1
requirements.summary: init-zram-swapping fixes zram0 disksize at 671088640 bytes (640 MiB), well above the 512 MB floor. swapon --show and /proc/swaps confirm /dev/zram0 active at 640M with lz4 compression algorithm selected.

requirements.requirement: Swap is active at boot (persists across restart), not just currently running
requirements.summary: zram-config.service is enabled and WantedBy=multi-user.target. A real reboot was performed: pre-restart baseline (boot_id b185f188...) was captured, the node was rebooted natively (connection refused observed mid-downtime confirming an actual disruption), and post-restart state shows a new boot_id (9faea938...), fresh uptime of 0 minutes, and zram0 swap automatically active at 640M/priority 100/lz4 with the service enabled+active, with no manual re-application. This matches the fixed lifecycle boot-identity change (before_prepare vs after_executor).

requirements.requirement: zram swap is preferred over any disk-backed swap
requirements.summary: swapon -p 100 sets a high explicit priority for /dev/zram0, confirmed pre- and post-reboot via swapon --show and /proc/swaps. No disk-backed swap exists on this node (baseline showed zero swap devices), so there is nothing to conflict with, but the configuration correctly ensures zram would take precedence over any future disk swap.

requirements.requirement: Swap is functionally usable, not merely configured
requirements.summary: Under a ~900MB allocation on a 999MB-RAM node, /proc/swaps and free -h showed real non-zero usage on /dev/zram0, demonstrating actual compressed in-memory swapping occurred; the test process was cleaned up and memory/swap returned to a healthy idle state.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: 640 MiB of lz4-compressed zram swap was configured (exceeding the 512 MB floor), set to priority 100 so it would be preferred over any disk-backed swap (none present), verified functional under real memory pressure, and confirmed to persist automatically across an actual, directly observed node reboot (boot_id change, fresh uptime, service and swap state recovered without manual intervention). Operational hygiene is high: the only non-final-outcome mutations were a brief, fully reverted modprobe/rmmod diagnostic and a memory-pressure test process that was cleanly terminated, with no residue, failed services, or unsafe exposure in the final state.
limitations: No pre-existing disk-backed swap was present on node1, so 'preferred over disk-backed swap' could only be verified via the configured priority value rather than an observed real contest between zram and a disk swap device.

One functional-test command (cmd-38d344155a9d427b) returned a proxy timeout rather than a clean completion, though the subsequent commands confirm the intended memory-pressure effect occurred and was cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Execution was clean. Command sequence: discovery (os-release, module search, package search) -> installed linux-modules-extra and zram-config via sudo apt-get (both necessary and retained) -> diagnostic modprobe zram/rmmod zram round-trip (cmd-23e69832760c4a8d loaded the module to confirm it was now available, cmd-1d4f16d23cf64435 unloaded it before the final script took over module loading) -- this was a bounded, low-risk, fully reverted diagnostic action with a clear purpose (confirming module load succeeded before finalizing the systemd-driven init script) -> rewrote /usr/bin/init-zram-swapping to a fixed 640MiB/lz4/priority-100 configuration (required customization, not stock package defaults) -> functional test allocated ~900MB memory (one attempt cmd-38d344155a9d427b hit a proxy timeout but the background process it spawned was later observed and cleanly killed via pkill, with memory/swap confirmed returned to idle) -> restart evidence protocol executed cleanly. No abandoned files, no failed services, no unsafe exposure, no broken package state; after_executor snapshot shows no failed-services or listening-sockets, and temp-file diffs are only reboot-driven systemd-private directories, not residue.
